summary: Heinrich August Eduard Schaeffer worked in Indology and religious studies. He studied at the University of Leipzig and served as Principal at the Evangelical Lutheran Central High School.

Heinrich August Jäschke worked in Tibetology and linguistics. Educated at Pädagogium Niesky and Gnadenfeld Theological Seminary, he taught at Christiansfeld Moravian School (1837–1842), co-directed Pädagogium Niesky (1842–1856), and was a missionary at Kyelang and the Moravian Church.

Heinrich Blatt was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Munich, Leipzig, Berlin, Würzburg, and Erlangen-Nuremberg, earning his Ph.D. by 1923. From 1923 to 1946, he served as a librarian at Würzburg University Library.

Heinrich Blochmann worked in Iranian and Central Asian studies, Indology, and history and archaeology. Educated at Leipzig, Paris, and Calcutta, he taught at Doveton College (1862–1864) and Aliah University, serving as Principal from 1865, and was Secretary of The Asiatic Society (1868–1878).
Heinrich Brunn was a scholar in history and archaeology who studied at the University of Bonn (around 1839–1843). He later held a post at the University of Munich from around 1865 to 1894.

Heinrich Düntzer worked in linguistics and Indology. He studied at the University of Bonn under Friedrich Gottlieb Welcker and at Humboldt University of Berlin under Franz Bopp. He held posts at the University of Bonn (circa 1836–1846) and Dreikönigsgymnasium (1846–1885).

Heinrich Ewald worked in linguistics, Indology, and religious studies, studying at the University of Göttingen under Thomas Christian Tychsen. He served as a professor at Göttingen (1824–1837, 1848–1867) and at the University of Tübingen (1838–1848).

Heinrich Franz Joseph Junker specialized in linguistics and Iranian and Central Asian studies. After studying at Giessen, Strasbourg, and Heidelberg under Christian Bartholomae, he held professorships at Hamburg (from 1919), Leipzig (1926–1945), and Humboldt University of Berlin (1951).
Heinrich Gustav Hotho worked in philosophy and other fields. He studied at Humboldt University of Berlin from around 1822 to 1826 and subsequently held a post there from around 1829 to 1873.
Heinrich Gössel was an Indologist who earned his Ph.D. at the University of Leipzig, studying under Ernst Windisch. In 1917, he served as an assistant at the University of Leipzig.

Heinrich Hackmann worked in Sinology, religious studies, and Buddhist studies. He studied at Leipzig, Göttingen, and Basel. He served as Privatdozent at Göttingen (circa 1893–1894) and as Professor of History of Religions at the University of Amsterdam (1913–1934).

Heinrich Hettrich worked in linguistics, Indology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Saarland, Giessen, and Munich. He taught at Salzburg, Zurich, and Marburg before becoming Chair of Comparative Linguistics at Würzburg in 1989.

Heinrich Hübschmann worked in linguistics, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and Indology. He studied at Jena, Tübingen, Munich under Martin Haug, and Leipzig. He was Privatdozent at Leipzig in 1875 and Professor of Comparative Linguistics at Strasbourg from 1877.

Heinrich Kiepert was a geographer and historian who studied at Berlin and Jena under Boeckh, Ranke, and Petermann. He led cartography at Geographisches Institut Weimar and Dietrich Reimer Verlag, and served as professor of geography at Berlin from 1859.

Heinrich Leberecht Fleischer worked in linguistics. He studied at Leipzig under Gottfried Hermann and in Paris under Silvestre de Sacy, Caussin de Perceval, Chézy, and Jaubert, later holding the chair of Oriental languages at Leipzig from 1836.

Heinrich Lüders was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Munich and Göttingen under Franz Kielhorn. He held the chair of Ancient Indian Language and Literature at Berlin (1909–1935) and served as Secretary of the Prussian Academy of Sciences (1920–1938).

Heinrich Meinhard worked in Indology, history, and archaeology. He earned his Ph.D. at the University of Bonn under Willibald Kirfel, served as curator at the Berlin Ethnological Museum (circa 1928–1937), and later became Reader in Anthropology at Durham University in 1950.

Heinrich Meyer-Benfey worked in Indology and German. He studied at the University of Göttingen (circa 1888–1893) and held posts at the University of Hamburg as Privatdozent (1919) and as associate professor of German (1923–1938).

Heinrich Nau was an Indologist. He studied at the University of Marburg, Concordia Seminary (circa 1901–1905), and the University of Halle (circa 1916–1920), where he earned his Ph.D. under Eugen Hultzsch.
Heinrich Plütschau was a scholar of Indology and linguistics. He studied theology at the University of Halle from around 1702 to 1705 and later held a post at the same institution.
